title: OET Speaking: The Two Role Plays
summary: OET Speaking's profession-specific role plays with an interlocutor — and the patient-centred communication skills that score.

nodes.label: Two role plays
nodes.note: Real healthcare scenarios for your profession

nodes.label: Prep time
nodes.note: A few minutes to read each role-play card

chunks.heading: Two profession-specific role plays
chunks.body: OET Speaking takes about **20 minutes** and centres on **two role plays** based on **real healthcare scenarios for your profession**. You play the **health professional**; an **interlocutor plays the patient, client or carer**. You get a **role-play card and short prep time** before each.
chunks.realExample: A nurse might reassure an anxious pre-op patient; a pharmacist might explain a new medication — you handle the scenario as you would at work, in English.
chunks.memoryHook: 20 min, 2 role plays. You're the professional; they're the patient. Read the card, then go.

chunks.heading: Use the prep card well
chunks.body: Each card gives your **role, the setting and the tasks** (explain, reassure, advise, gather information). Use the **prep time to note your tasks** so you cover them all — missing a required task costs marks even if your English is fluent.
chunks.realExample: If the card says explain the diagnosis, address the patient's worry, and agree next steps, plan to hit all three — a fluent chat that skips 'agree next steps' is incomplete.
chunks.memoryHook: The card lists your tasks. Note them, then cover every one.

chunks.heading: Communicate like a real clinician
chunks.body: OET rewards **patient-centred communication**: **listen and respond to the patient's concerns, explain in plain language, show empathy, and check understanding**. It's not a monologue — it's a two-way, professional conversation.
chunks.realExample: Rather than reciting facts, acknowledge the worry ('I understand this is stressful'), explain simply, and ask 'does that make sense?' — the human, clinical skills are being assessed too.
chunks.memoryHook: Listen, explain simply, show empathy, check understanding. It's a conversation, not a speech.

chunks.heading: Two assessment lenses
chunks.body: You're marked on **linguistic criteria** (intelligibility, fluency, grammar and vocabulary) **and clinical-communication criteria** (relationship-building, understanding the patient's perspective, structuring the interaction). **Clear, natural English** plus **good bedside manner** together produce a strong grade.
chunks.realExample: Fluent English with poor rapport, or great rapport with unclear English, both fall short — the top grades need both the language and the patient-care communication.
chunks.memoryHook: Two lenses: your English AND your clinical communication. You need both.

recall.q: What is the core of the OET Speaking sub-test?
recall.a: Two profession-specific role plays (about 20 minutes total) based on real healthcare scenarios, with an interlocutor playing the patient or carer.

recall.q: Who do you play in the role plays?
recall.a: The health professional, while the interlocutor plays the patient, client or carer.

recall.q: How should you use the prep time before each role play?
recall.a: Read the role-play card and note your required tasks so you cover all of them.

recall.q: What communication skills does OET Speaking reward?
recall.a: Patient-centred communication — listening to concerns, explaining in plain language, showing empathy and checking understanding.

recall.q: On what two sets of criteria is OET Speaking assessed?
recall.a: Linguistic criteria (intelligibility, fluency, grammar, vocabulary) and clinical-communication criteria (relationship-building, patient perspective, structuring the interaction).
